title.en: A Good Name Is Better Than Riches

heading.en: Wealth that grows wings and flies away

body.en:
'Those who trust in their riches will fall, but the righteous will thrive like a green leaf.' Proverbs is honest about the danger of putting too much confidence in money — it simply isn't sturdy enough to lean on fully.

'Better a little with righteousness than much gain with injustice.' Quantity isn't the point — Proverbs consistently cares more about HOW wealth is gained than how much of it exists.

One of the most countercultural verses in the whole book: 'a good name is more desirable than great riches; to be esteemed is better than silver or gold.' Character and reputation, Proverbs insists, outweigh wealth itself.

'The rich rule over the poor, and the borrower is servant to the lender.' Proverbs is realistic about how money creates power dynamics, encouraging wisdom about debt and financial dependence.

A vivid warning closes this theme: 'do not wear yourself out to get rich; do not trust your own cleverness. Cast but a glance at riches, and they are gone, for they will surely sprout wings and fly off, like an eagle, into the sky.' Wealth, Proverbs warns, is far less permanent than it appears.

verse.en: A good name is more desirable than great riches; to be esteemed is better than silver or gold.

title.en: A Song for A Good Name Is Better Than Riches

q.en: According to Proverbs 22:1, what is more desirable than great riches?
What does Proverbs 11:28 say happens to those who trust in their riches?

en: They will fall; the righteous thrive like a green leaf instead

q.en: What vivid image does Proverbs 23:4-5 use to describe how quickly wealth can disappear?

en: Riches sprout wings and fly off like an eagle into the sky

label.en: Activity sheet: A Good Name Is Better Than Riches

body.en:
Big idea: Proverbs consistently relativizes wealth — never condemning it outright, but repeatedly warning against trusting in it, valuing it above character, or pursuing it at the expense of integrity. The vivid image of riches "sprouting wings" captures money's genuine instability, a needed corrective in any culture (ancient or modern) that tends to overvalue financial security.

Conversation starters: (1) Why might a "good name" — your character and reputation — actually matter more than wealth? (2) What does it mean that riches can "sprout wings and fly away" — how have you seen this happen, even to wealthy people? (3) How does HOW money is earned matter, not just how much is earned?

Pray for hearts that value character over wealth, and wisdom about how money is pursued and used.
